explanations.answer: Bound on his heart and tied around his neck
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The teacher says, "Bind them always upon your heart; tie them around your neck." Heart AND neck. That's not a sticky note on the fridge, that's wearing the thing. I can lose a recipe card in my own apron pocket, so I respect this level of closeness.

explanations.answer: Written on the doorframe of his house
explanations.explanation: Nice try, but the teacher never mentions a doorframe here. He says to bind the teaching on the heart and tie it around the neck (Proverbs 6:21). Think about it, friend. A doorframe stays home when you leave, and a neck goes EVERYWHERE you go.

explanations.answer: Kept on a scroll beside his bed
explanations.explanation: No scroll and no bedside table in this verse, baker. The teacher says to bind it "…upon your heart…" and tie it "…around your neck." (Proverbs 6:21) A scroll by the bed is a great plan right up until you leave the bedroom.

That's right. The teacher says, "when you lie down, they will watch over you…" So even when the son lies down, the teaching is still on the job. Some folks can't even keep an eye on the clock while they're awake, so that's impressive.

This one is true, baker. The teacher says, "when you lie down, they will watch over you…" That's right in the middle of a list. When the son walks, they guide him, when he lies down, they watch over him, and when he wakes, they speak to him. So the father's commandment and the mother's teaching keep working all day and all night.

Yes, baker. The teacher says "…the reproofs of discipline are the way to life…" (Proverbs 6:23). Correction can sting a little, but it points the right way. Right next to the lamp and the light, it keeps the son walking toward life.

Honor sounds like a good guess, friend. But the teacher says the reproofs of discipline are "…the way to life…" That's the word he chose, and it's a big one. Honor can wait while we all say hello to life first.

I hear you, baker. Riches sound great, and I wouldn't mind a few extra chocolate chips myself. But the teacher says the reproofs of discipline are "…the way to life…" He doesn't say a word about riches there.

explanations.answer: The evil woman with a smooth tongue
explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. The teaching is there "…to keep you from the evil woman, from the smooth tongue of the adulteress." Notice it's her smooth tongue that gets the warning.

explanations.answer: The slacker who sleeps all day
explanations.explanation: Ha, a good guess, baker, but the teacher isn't talking about a napper here. The teaching is meant "…to keep you from the evil woman, from the smooth tongue of the adulteress." That's the person he names in this passage. I love a nap, but nobody in these verses is getting warned about one.

explanations.answer: The stranger who asks for a pledge
explanations.explanation: Close to home for a Proverbs reader, friend, but not this passage. Here the teacher says the teaching is "…to keep you from the evil woman, from the smooth tongue of the adulteress." Nobody in these verses is asking for a pledge. It's the adulteress, and her smooth tongue, he warns about.

Careful, baker, this one slips by. The teacher also warns about what's going on inside the son. He says, "Do not lust in your heart for her beauty…" So it's about the heart, not just the hands and feet.

That's right. The teacher says, "Do not lust in your heart for her beauty…" That's a warning about the heart, not just about what the son does. He's talking about what the son wants inside before anything shows on the outside.

You got it, baker. The teacher says, "Do not lust in your heart for her beauty or let her captivate you with her eyes." Beauty and eyes, those are the two. Eyes are tricky, friend. I once stared at one cookie for ten minutes and forgot the rest of the batch.

Not here, baker. The teacher doesn't say a thing about her money or her house. He says, "Do not lust in your heart for her beauty or let her captivate you with her eyes." The pull he names is her beauty and her eyes.

Her family and friends never show up in this verse, friend. The teacher says, "Do not lust in your heart for her beauty or let her captivate you with her eyes." So the two things are her beauty and her eyes. Nobody's getting warned about a guest list.

That's right, baker. The teacher says, "…the adulteress preys upon your very life." Your very life, not just your pocket. He's not whispering a small warning here. He's telling the son how much is at stake.

Actually the teacher says exactly that. The verse says, "…the adulteress preys upon your very life." Right before it, he mentions the levy of the prostitute is poverty. So he's talking about a cost much bigger than loose change, friend.

Hold on, baker, that's the opposite. The teacher asks, "Can a man embrace fire and his clothes not be burned?" It's a question with an obvious answer, and the answer is no. Hugging a hot oven is not a plan I recommend, and my apron and I have history.

Yes, that's it. The teacher asks, "Can a man embrace fire and his clothes not be burned?" He's asking something everybody already knows. Hold fire close and you get burned, baker. Nobody needs a long lecture about it.
Right, baker. The teacher says, "no one who touches her will go unpunished." He's talking about the man who sleeps with another man's wife. After the fire and the hot coals, this is where he lands.

The teacher says the opposite, friend. He says, "no one who touches her will go unpunished." That comes right after the fire and the hot coals. So he's saying it won't go unpunished, not that it will slide by.

That's right, baker. The teacher says, "Yet if caught, he must pay sevenfold…" And that's for a thief who stole because he was hungry. So if even that thief pays a heavy price, you can see where the teacher is going with the adulterer.

explanations.answer: He is let go and forgiven
explanations.explanation: Not in this verse, friend. The teacher says, "Yet if caught, he must pay sevenfold…" Men don't despise that thief, but he still has to pay. So no, he isn't just waved off.

explanations.answer: He pays back just what he took
explanations.explanation: Closer, baker, but the teacher goes bigger. He says, "Yet if caught, he must pay sevenfold…" Sevenfold means seven times over. If I stole one cookie and owed seven, I'd be baking all night.
That's right for the first blank. The teacher says, "He who commits adultery lacks judgment…" He's saying the man isn't thinking clearly.
You've got the second blank. The teacher says, "whoever does so destroys himself." Not a stranger, not a rival. The damage lands on the man himself. That's a heavy line, friend.

Good guess, baker, but it's not what the verse says. The teacher says the man who commits adultery "lacks judgment." Judgment is the thing missing, not courage. I'd say this takes the opposite of wisdom, not a lack of nerve.
Not quite, friend. The teacher says, "whoever does so destroys himself." The man ends up as the one who gets hurt. This line points back at him, not out at strangers.
Rivals are a fun guess, baker, but the verse points inward. The teacher says, "whoever does so destroys himself." It's himself that the man destroys. No rival has to lift a finger.
That's it, baker. The teacher says, "For jealousy enrages a husband…" Jealousy is the word he picks. He also says the husband "…will show no mercy in the day of vengeance."
Greed is a good guess, friend, but it isn't the word here. The teacher says, "For jealousy enrages a husband…" So the husband's anger comes from jealousy. Greed doesn't get a mention.
Pride is a fair guess, baker, but the teacher picked another word. He says, "For jealousy enrages a husband…" That's the cause he names. He doesn't say anything about pride in this verse.
Careful, baker, the teacher says the opposite. The husband "…will not be appeased by any ransom, or persuaded by lavish gifts." That means no big payment calms him down.

You've got it. The teacher says, "He will not be appeased by any ransom, or persuaded by lavish gifts." So no amount of gifts settles things in the day of vengeance. He's showing how serious it is, baker.
